Historical observations for this pairing were gathered by the National Snow and Ice Data Center using satellite imaging technology and data processing methods developed by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration. These observations begin in 1979, when routine monitoring by satellites started.

Model outputs are based on a set of 16 global climate models that reflect scientists’ current understanding of how greenhouse gases warm the atmosphere; how this heat moves between the atmosphere, water, and land; and how these changes influence the air and water temperatures that allow ice to form and remain in the Arctic Ocean. These same 16 models were used in the most recent National Climate Assessment. The modeled lines are smoother than the historical trends because the project team averaged 16 models together and also applied an 11-year smoothing filter, both of which smooth out year-to-year variability. However, the shaded bands do include year-to-year variability.

When comparing observed and modeled data, the models underestimated actual Arctic sea ice extent. This results in part because different grid cell sizes lead to different results (see technical documentation). The project team corrected this bias by shifting all model outputs by a consistent ratio so the average model hindcast would align with average observed results for the years where they coincide, 1979–2014.

Sea ice extent is defined as the area of ocean where at least 15 percent of the surface is frozen. This threshold was chosen because scientists have found that it gives the best approximation of the edge of the ice. While data are collected throughout the year, this indicator focuses on the month when sea ice typically reaches its minimum extent. That typically happens in September after melting during the spring and summer.
